<reason>Both sides argued with discipline and landed genuine clash, but Side A controlled the decisive axis of the debate: the distinction between coastal militarization (where the real danger B cites actually occurs) and the empty high-seas/Ridge pocket (the only zone B's narrowed treaty would actually govern). Once B conceded in Rebuttal 1 that the treaty would not touch inhabited coasts, Alaska, or Kola, A repeatedly and effectively pointed out that this leaves B's own evidence of danger (Russian coastal base expansion, NATO response, the flag stunt) completely unaddressed by B's actual proposal. B's closing never squarely answered this evidence-scope mismatch, instead re-asserting that the unresolved pocket itself is dangerous without reconnecting that claim to the militarization evidence A had cleanly separated out in A4.1. B's "removes the finish line" metaphor and "resolves what nobody owns" framing were strong rhetorical moves and did expose a real tension in A's "clear ownership prevents incidents" logic, but A's answer (low stakes plus functioning slow diplomacy) was a reasonable, consistently maintained response that was never fully dislodged. A's Pressure Questions also extracted the scope-narrowing clarification that became the fulcrum A exploited for the rest of the debate, showing strong progression and use of the format. On balance, A gave the clearer, more consistently reinforced path to a verdict.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's repeated "coastal militarization vs. empty pocket" distinction (first surfaced in A2.3, sharpened in A4.1, and closed out in A5.2) which exposed that B's alarming evidence never actually matched the narrow scope of B's own proposed treaty, and which B's closing did not directly rebut.</best_rebuttal>
